summary:
Ley 4/2023, published on 28 February 2023, grants legal gender recognition on self-identification. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry before the Civil Registry, without the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The reform places the state alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in permitting administrative self-declaration.

Gender identity is an explicit aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and courts are applying it. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

No legal rule restricts a trans visitor's use of facilities matching their presentation. The framework remains centred on gender self-determination, in contrast to the United Kingdom, where the EHRC statutory code moves toward single-sex spaces defined on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Acceptance is high in major cities and tourist centres, where LGBTQ communities and social venues are established, and more conservative outside them. The UK government's travel advice describes the state as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities, and Intrepid Travel rates it safe and welcoming while advising travellers to know local conditions before going, including venue-by-venue and regional variation.

The national tourism institute markets the country through eight flagship LGBTQ+ destinations and a "Destinations for Diversity" certification denoting open, safe, welcoming and discrimination-free spaces.
tangentialFactors:
Facility access for trans travellers now diverges between neighbouring jurisdictions: the United Kingdom is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code, while the state retains a legal framework built on gender self-determination. The practical difference concerns which side of a border a traveller is on when entering a bathroom.

On gender recognition, the state sits with Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay among countries that have adopted self-identification, and is described in overview sources as one of the world's most LGBT-friendly countries.

A 23-country survey from December 2016 ranked the state the most trans-supportive of the group: the only country where a majority supported unrestricted change of legal gender designation, one of three where restroom support exceeded 70% alongside Argentina and India, and a country where 25% of respondents said they knew a trans person. The survey predates the 2023 law.

Trip-planning reference points named by the national tourism institute are Madrid (Chueca), Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, the Canary Islands (Maspalomas Pride), Sitges and Torremolinos (La Nogalera).
localsOnly:
Registry rectification runs through the Civil Registry under Article 43 for applicants aged 16 and over acting on their own request; the same law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in place since 2005, alongside legal gender change without surgery or sterilisation, LGBTQ military service and MSM blood donation from the same year.

Ley 4/2023 also expands assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans non-consensual "normalising" surgeries on intersex children, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and adds anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing.

The statutory division of labour matters when reading enforcement: the hate-speech aggravation in Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code and the penalties in Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a six- to twelve-month fine) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 reformed offences against sexual freedom in Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.
outOfScopeNotes:
Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, and gender-identity-motivated hate crime has no free-standing offence; it operates as an aggravating circumstance applied within other offences, which shapes how cases are charged and reported.

The public-attitude baseline is a December 2016 survey, seven years older than the statute it is read against, and its country rankings have not been refreshed in this inventory.

The historical timeline in this record rests on a tertiary encyclopedic overview rather than primary legislation for the 2005 milestones.

Enforcement evidence is thin: one first-instance misdemeanour fine in Vigo and one adult prison sentence in Valencia with two minors judged separately. Whether the aggravation is applied routinely beyond these cases is not established here.

Official UK travel advice pairs its tolerant-and-progressive framing with standard crime warnings unrelated to gender identity, including that counterfeit money is treated as a serious offence.
